blogs.title: Modern Kitchen Design Ideas for Pakistani Homes
blogs.description: Modern kitchen design ideas for Pakistani homes: layouts, cabinet materials, countertops, ventilation and small kitchen tips from SEECA's interior designers.
blogs.content:
A kitchen is the hardest-working room in a Pakistani home. It handles daily tarka and frying, large family meals and guests arriving at short notice, all in a climate that brings summer heat, monsoon humidity and dust. Good kitchen design is not only about how the kitchen looks on the day it is finished, but about how it performs after years of real cooking.

This guide covers the decisions that matter most when you plan a modern kitchen in Pakistan: layout, cabinet materials, countertops, ventilation, storage and lighting. It draws on how our interior designers at SEECA plan kitchens for homes in Lahore and beyond.

## Start with how your family really cooks

Before choosing colours or cabinet finishes, list how the kitchen will be used. Desi cooking produces heat, smoke and grease, so extraction and easy-to-clean surfaces come first. Ask a few practical questions:

- Who cooks, and how often: the family, a cook, or both?
- Do you cook in large quantities for guests or events?
- Do you need a separate "dirty kitchen" for heavy cooking, with a cleaner show kitchen for tea, breakfast and serving?
- Where will the fridge, microwave, oven, water dispenser and dishwasher go?

Many larger homes in Pakistan now plan two kitchens: a main working kitchen near the service area and a lighter, open kitchen or pantry connected to the family lounge. If your plot allows it, this keeps smells and grease away from the living spaces while still giving you a beautiful kitchen to show.

## Choose the right kitchen layout

The layout decides how comfortable the kitchen is to work in. Designers often think in terms of the "work triangle" between the sink, the hob and the fridge: these three points should be close enough to move between easily, without people crossing each other's paths.

- **L-shaped kitchen:** the most flexible layout for medium-sized kitchens. It keeps the work triangle compact and leaves space for a small dining table or breakfast counter.
- **U-shaped kitchen:** cabinets on three sides give the most storage and counter space, which suits families who cook a lot.
- **Parallel (galley) kitchen:** two facing runs of cabinets. It is efficient for narrow spaces and works well as a dedicated working kitchen.
- **Kitchen with an island:** an island adds preparation space, storage and casual seating. It needs a larger room, with roughly a metre of clear space around it so drawers and doors open comfortably.
- **Peninsula kitchen:** a counter attached to one wall instead of a free-standing island, a good option when the room is too small for a full island.

## Kitchen cabinet design: materials that last in Pakistan

Kitchen cabinet design is where most of the budget goes, and where cheap choices show their age fastest. Every cabinet has two parts to think about: the box (carcass) and the shutters (doors and drawer fronts).

### The cabinet box

The carcass sits near the sink, the dishwasher and spills, so moisture resistance matters. Ordinary MDF swells if water gets into it. Moisture-resistant boards such as HDHMR or good-quality plywood are a safer choice for the base cabinets, especially around the sink.

### Shutter finishes

- **Acrylic and high-gloss lacquer:** sleek and reflective, popular in modern kitchens. They look premium but show fingerprints and fine scratches.
- **Laminate and matte finishes:** practical, durable and available in many colours and wood textures. Matte finishes hide fingerprints better.
- **Wood veneer:** natural grain and warmth. It needs good sealing and care around heat and water.
- **Two-tone kitchens:** for example, wood-tone tall units with lighter base cabinets, or a deep colour on the island. This is one of the easiest ways to make a kitchen feel custom.

### Hardware

Good hinges, drawer runners and lift-up mechanisms make a bigger difference to daily use than most people expect. Soft-close hinges and full-extension drawers are worth the investment, because deep drawers are easier to use than deep cupboards for pots and pans.

## Countertops: granite, quartz or marble?

- **Granite:** a natural stone that handles heat well and suits heavy desi cooking. It is widely available in Pakistan in many colours.
- **Quartz:** engineered stone with a consistent look and strong stain resistance. It is low-maintenance, but very hot pans should go on a trivet.
- **Marble:** beautiful and classic, but it is softer and reacts to acids such as lemon, vinegar and tomato, leaving dull marks. It suits a show kitchen better than a heavy-use cooking counter.
- **Sintered stone and porcelain slabs:** a newer option with high resistance to heat, scratches and stains, available in large, thin slabs.

A common approach is to use a hard-wearing stone in the working kitchen and a more decorative surface on the island or breakfast counter.

## Ventilation: the most important part of a Pakistani kitchen

Without strong extraction, grease and smoke settle on cabinets, walls and ceilings, and smells spread through the house. Plan ventilation at the design stage, not after the cabinets are installed:

- Use a ducted chimney hood that vents outside, not a recirculating one, for regular desi cooking.
- Plan the duct route early, so it can run neatly through the ceiling or a wall to the outside.
- Match the hood width to the hob, and place it at the height the manufacturer recommends.
- Add a window or a separate exhaust fan for cross-ventilation, especially in a dirty kitchen.

## Small kitchen design ideas

A small kitchen can work as well as a large one if every centimetre is planned:

- Run cabinets to the ceiling to gain storage and avoid dust on top.
- Use light colours, matte finishes and handleless or slim handles to keep the room visually calm.
- Add pull-out larder units, corner carousels and drawer organisers instead of deep, hard-to-reach cupboards.
- Choose a slimmer hob, an integrated fridge or a built-in microwave to free counter space.
- Light the countertops with under-cabinet LED strips, so the work surface is never in shadow.

## Modular kitchen vs custom-built kitchen

A modular kitchen is built from factory-made units in standard sizes and assembled on site. It is quick to install and the quality is consistent. A custom-built kitchen is designed for your exact room, so it uses awkward corners, odd ceiling heights and columns fully and can include details such as appliance garages or a coffee station.

Many homes combine both: standard modules for the base and wall cabinets, and custom pieces for the island, tall units and storage walls. At SEECA we design custom kitchens as part of our [interior design services](/interior-design) and plan every unit in 3D before production starts.

## Lighting a modern kitchen

Plan three layers of light: general ceiling light for the whole room, task lighting under the wall cabinets and over the hob, and accent lighting such as pendants over the island or lit glass cabinets. Warm white light makes wood and stone look inviting, while neutral white is better for the main working area.

## Kitchen design trends in Pakistani homes for 2026

- **Warm wood with stone:** walnut or oak-tone cabinets with light quartz or sintered stone counters.
- **Deeper colours:** sage green, olive and charcoal on islands or lower cabinets, paired with lighter upper units.
- **Islands with seating:** the island becomes a breakfast counter and a place for the family to gather.
- **Hidden storage:** tall pantry units, appliance garages and handleless fronts that keep counters clear.
- **Integrated appliances:** built-in ovens, microwaves and fridges for a clean, continuous look.

You can see some of these ideas in our projects. The [Ambreen Residence in Lahore](/portfolio/ambreen-residence-lahore) combines walnut cabinetry with a white breakfast bar and sage-green stools, and a [vacation villa in the Turks and Caicos Islands](/portfolio/vocational-villa-turks-and-caicos-island) is built around light oak joinery and a white marble island.

## How SEECA designs a kitchen

Our process follows the same four steps as every SEECA project. We start with a brief about how you cook and live, plan the layout and budget together, and then prepare photorealistic 3D renders and detailed working drawings for every cabinet, so you can approve the look before anything is made. If you choose design and build, our team also handles the fit-out. You can read more about [our design and build process](/our-process) or [see our projects](/portfolio).

## Frequently asked questions

### How much space do I need for a kitchen island?

As a guide, leave about one metre of clear space on every side of the island, so people can pass and cabinet doors and drawers can open. If the room is narrower, a peninsula is usually the better option.

### Which kitchen cabinet material is best for Pakistan's climate?

For the cabinet boxes, especially under the sink, choose moisture-resistant boards such as HDHMR or good-quality plywood over ordinary MDF. For the doors, laminate and matte finishes are the most practical, while acrylic and lacquer give a more polished look with a little more care.

### Is marble a good choice for a kitchen countertop?

Marble is beautiful but marks easily with acidic foods such as lemon and tomato. For a kitchen used for daily desi cooking, granite, quartz or sintered stone are more practical, and marble can be used on an island or in a show kitchen.

### Should I have a separate dirty kitchen?

If you cook often and your home has the space, yes. A separate working kitchen keeps heavy cooking, smells and grease away from the open kitchen and living areas.

blogs.title: 1 Kanal House Design in Lahore: Plans & Elevations
blogs.description: Planning a 1 kanal house in Lahore? Plot size, building rules, house plans, front elevation design ideas and common mistakes, from SEECA architects.
blogs.content:
A 1 kanal plot is the point where a house in Lahore can truly be designed around your family: room for a proper entrance, generous living spaces, five or more bedrooms and a front elevation that makes a statement. It is also a large investment, so the early design decisions matter.

This guide explains how to plan a 1 kanal house design in Lahore, from plot size and planning rules to layouts, front elevation styles and the mistakes to avoid. It is based on how SEECA's architects approach residential projects across Lahore and Pakistan.

## How big is a 1 kanal plot?

In Lahore's housing societies, one kanal equals 20 marla. With the 225 sq ft marla used in most societies, that is about 4,500 sq ft of land. Plot proportions vary by society: a 1 kanal plot in DHA Lahore is typically around 45 × 100 ft, while in Bahria Town Lahore it is often around 50 × 90 ft.

Some older areas and revenue records use a larger marla, so always check the exact dimensions on your plot documents before design starts. The width, depth and which side faces the road all shape the final plan.

## Check the building rules before you design

Every society and authority (such as DHA, Bahria Town or LDA) has its own building by-laws. They control:

- **Setbacks:** the open space required at the front, back and sides of the plot.
- **Ground coverage:** how much of the plot the house can cover.
- **Height and number of storeys:** including rules for the roof and mumty.
- **Basements:** whether a basement is allowed and how it must be built.
- **Car parking, boundary walls and gates.**

A good architect designs within these rules from the start, so the drawings can be approved without major changes later.

## A typical 1 kanal house layout

Every family is different, but most 1 kanal house plans in Lahore follow a similar pattern across two storeys, with an optional basement.

### Ground floor

- Covered car porch for two or more cars
- Formal drawing room and dining area near the entrance, for guests
- Family lounge, often with a double-height space or connection to the garden
- Main kitchen, with a separate working (dirty) kitchen in many homes
- One guest bedroom with an attached bathroom, useful for elderly parents
- Powder room, store and a servant room with its own access

### First floor

- Master bedroom suite with a dressing area and an attached bathroom
- Two or three more bedrooms, each with an attached bathroom
- A family or TV lounge for the private part of the house
- A terrace or balcony overlooking the front or rear lawn

### Basement (optional)

- Home theatre, gym or games room
- Additional guest suite or storage

In total, a 1 kanal house usually has five to six bedrooms, and more with a basement.

## Planning principles for a better 1 kanal house

### Design for Lahore's climate

Lahore summers are long and hot. Orient living spaces to avoid harsh western sun, add deep overhangs, shaded windows and terraces, and use courtyards or double-height spaces to bring in daylight and air. Good planning can noticeably reduce cooling loads and energy bills. Our [sustainable building design](/building-sustainability) work focuses on exactly these decisions.

### Separate guest and family zones

Pakistani homes host guests often. Placing the drawing and dining rooms near the entrance, with the family lounge and bedrooms further in or upstairs, gives the family privacy while still welcoming guests properly.

### Give the staircase and entrance room to breathe

The staircase and entrance hall are the first spaces people experience. A generous, well-lit stair, often in a double-height volume, makes a 1 kanal house feel open and premium. The [1 kanal residence in Bahria Town](/portfolio/mr-faraz-ali-1-kanal-id-bahria-town-lahore) that our team designed uses a dramatic double-height entrance with a veined stone feature wall.

### Plan services from day one

Air-conditioner outdoor units, water tanks, solar panels, generator or UPS space and future lift shafts all need a place. When they are planned early, they are hidden neatly instead of cluttering the roof and elevation.

### Storage everywhere

Walk-in wardrobes, linen cupboards, a pantry near the kitchen and a proper store room keep the house uncluttered for years.

## Front elevation design ideas for a 1 kanal house

The front elevation is the face of your house and one of the most searched parts of house design. The best elevations come from the plan rather than being added on top of it. Popular directions in Lahore include:

## Check the building rules before you design

Every society and authority (such as DHA, Bahria Town or LDA) has its own building by-laws. They control:

- **Setbacks:** the open space required at the front, back and sides of the plot.
- **Ground coverage:** how much of the plot the house can cover.
- **Height and number of storeys:** including rules for the roof and mumty.
- **Basements:** whether a basement is allowed and how it must be built.
- **Car parking, boundary walls and gates.**

A good architect designs within these rules from the start, so the drawings can be approved without major changes later.

- Covered car porch for two or more cars
- Formal drawing room and dining area near the entrance, for guests
- Family lounge, often with a double-height space or connection to the garden
- Main kitchen, with a separate working (dirty) kitchen in many homes
- One guest bedroom with an attached bathroom, useful for elderly parents
- Powder room, store and a servant room with its own access

### First floor

- Master bedroom suite with a dressing area and an attached bathroom
- Two or three more bedrooms, each with an attached bathroom
- A family or TV lounge for the private part of the house
- A terrace or balcony overlooking the front or rear lawn

### Basement (optional)

- Home theatre, gym or games room

Pakistani homes host guests often. Placing the drawing and dining rooms near the entrance, with the family lounge and bedrooms further in or upstairs, gives the family privacy while still welcoming guests properly.

Air-conditioner outdoor units, water tanks, solar panels, generator or UPS space and future lift shafts all need a place. When they are planned early, they are hidden neatly instead of cluttering the roof and elevation.

blogs.title: Smart Building Technologies That Quietly Improve Daily Life
blogs.description: SEECA integrates intelligent systems for comfort, security, and efficiency — technology that supports the building without overwhelming the people inside it.
blogs.content:
Smart buildings succeed when technology disappears into better daily experiences. At SEECA, we integrate systems that improve comfort, safety, and efficiency while keeping interfaces simple and spaces visually calm.

Our approach starts with the building’s real operational needs: lighting scenes, climate zones, access control, monitoring, and energy visibility. Instead of stacking disconnected gadgets, we plan an architecture for data and control — so systems can communicate, scale, and remain maintainable over time.

In commercial and mixed-use projects, this often means intelligent access, wayfinding, occupancy-aware lighting, and dashboards that help facility teams act quickly. In residential work, the priority is quieter: scenes that respond to time of day, security that feels seamless, and climate control that stays out of the way.

Technology should never compete with materials and light. When smart systems are designed as part of the architecture from the beginning, they raise performance without turning the building into a showroom of screens. The best smart building feels intuitive, efficient, and human.

blogs.title: Building Sustainability as a Design Responsibility
blogs.description: SEECA integrates energy performance, healthy materials, and climate-responsive strategies so sustainability is built into the project — not added as a label.
blogs.content:
Sustainability is not a separate service layer at SEECA. It is a design responsibility that shapes orientation, envelope performance, material selection, and the way a building uses energy and water over its lifetime.

We begin with passive strategies whenever possible: daylighting, shading, natural ventilation potential, and thermal mass. These decisions reduce mechanical demand before equipment is ever specified. From there, we look at efficient systems, renewable opportunities, and durable assemblies that lower both operating cost and environmental impact.

Material choices matter as much as systems. We prefer finishes and assemblies that are healthy, locally appropriate where feasible, and resilient under real climate conditions. Green infrastructure — living walls, thoughtful landscaping, and water-conscious design — can also improve comfort while supporting biodiversity around the building.

A sustainable building should feel better to occupy, not only score better on paper. When performance and experience move together, sustainability becomes a lasting part of the architecture rather than a temporary claim.

blogs.title: Construction Built on Precision, Coordination, and Craft
blogs.description: From structural framing to final finishes, SEECA construction delivers architectural intent with disciplined site execution and clear project control.
blogs.content:
Design only becomes real when it is built well. SEECA’s construction approach is grounded in coordination, sequencing, and an insistence that drawings and site work stay aligned from groundbreaking to handover.

Every project begins with a clear build plan: structural logic, material lead times, trade dependencies, and quality checkpoints. We treat the site as a place of craft, not just logistics. Steel, concrete, envelope systems, and finishes are installed with the same attention we give to the design itself.

Communication is as important as construction. Clients, consultants, and contractors need shared visibility into progress, decisions, and risks. That transparency keeps schedules honest and protects the integrity of the original concept when field conditions demand adaptation.

Our teams focus on the details that decide whether a building feels carefully made — alignment, tolerances, waterproofing, and the handoff between structure and finish. When construction is disciplined, architecture holds its shape for decades.

blogs.title: Interior Design That Turns Space Into Experience
blogs.description: SEECA interiors are crafted around light, material, and movement — spaces that feel refined, livable, and unmistakably complete.
blogs.content:
Interior design is where architecture becomes personal. At SEECA, we shape rooms that feel composed from the moment you enter — balanced in proportion, warm in material, and clear in purpose.

Our process begins with how people actually move through a space. Circulation, seating, storage, and sightlines are planned together so the interior never feels like decoration applied after the fact. Every surface has a role: wood for warmth, stone for permanence, textiles for comfort, and carefully placed lighting for mood across the day.

We favor calm palettes with intentional contrast. Instead of filling rooms with objects, we edit carefully — choosing fewer pieces with stronger presence. Custom millwork, layered lighting, and tactile finishes give each project a quiet signature without visual noise.

Whether we are designing a private residence or a commercial interior, the goal is the same: a space that feels finished, functional, and ready to be lived in. Good interior design should not demand attention. It should reward it.

blogs.title: Architecture That Shapes How People Live and Work
blogs.description: How SEECA approaches architectural design as a balance of form, function, and place — creating buildings that feel intentional from the first sketch to the final detail.
blogs.content:
Great architecture begins long before the first wall is drawn. At SEECA, we treat every project as a conversation between site, climate, culture, and the people who will inhabit the finished space.

We start by reading the land carefully: orientation, views, circulation, and the surrounding fabric of the neighborhood. Those conditions become the foundation for a clear design concept — one that is strong enough to guide decisions and flexible enough to evolve as the brief unfolds.

Form follows purpose, but never at the expense of atmosphere. Our architectural work looks for quiet clarity: well-proportioned volumes, honest materials, and daylight that does real work. We design for longevity, so buildings remain relevant as uses change and cities grow around them.

From concept sketches to construction documentation, we stay close to the details that make architecture feel considered — thresholds, overhangs, structural rhythm, and the way a facade meets the sky. The result is architecture that does more than look resolved. It supports daily life with calm precision.
